headline_claim: "Overall, our results suggest that fixed-size chunking remains a more efficient and reliable choice for practical RAG applications." (p. 4, Conclusion)
evidence_location: Sec. 3.1-3.3 (p. 3); App. B hyperparameters (p. 7); App. D metrics (p. 9)
version_coded: NAACL Findings 2025 (ACL Anthology 2025.findings-naacl.114); protocol passages identical to arXiv v1
notes: Best hyperparameter configuration chosen per chunker by mean F1 over k; breakpoint chunker's chunk size is not tunable (p. 7), so arm lengths are uncontrolled and unreported. Evidence F1 includes precision, which partly penalises extra retrieved text. Significance tests reported only for embedding-model comparisons (App. E.2), not for chunkers.

headline_claim: "smaller chunks (64-128 tokens) are optimal for datasets with concise, fact-based answers, whereas larger chunks (512-1024 tokens) improve retrieval in datasets requiring broader contextual understanding" (p. 1, Abstract)
notes: Arms are fixed chunk sizes 64/128/256/512/1024 tokens compared by Recall@k with the same k, so at k=1 the 1024-token arm retrieves 16x the text of the 64-token arm. Two embedding models; four of six datasets are stitched synthetic documents.

headline_claim: "The strongest EM configuration in the baseline grid was chunk size 120 with top k=3, for both rerank off and rerank on." (p. 6, Sec. 5.3)
evidence_location: Sec. 3.3 chunking, 3.6 packing (pp. 3-4); Sec. 4.1 design (p. 4); Table 4 (p. 6)
notes: Full factorial chunk size {80,100,120,140} x top-k {2..5} x rerank; packed generation context capped at ~452 tokens, which partly bounds text at generation but not at retrieval (Hit@k at equal k). Packed token counts reported (Table 4 by k; Fig. 5). SD across 3 seeds only for noise/stability runs; chunk-size contrasts have no uncertainty. Single dataset.

n_queries_per_dataset: GutenQA 3,000; BEIR test sets (counts not stated)
headline_claim: "optimal chunking strategies are task-dependent: simple structure-based methods outperform LLM-guided alternatives for in-corpus retrieval, while LumberChunker performs best for in-document retrieval" (p. 1, Abstract)
evidence_location: Sec. 3.1, 3.3 (pp. 5-6); significance markers Tables 3/5 (pp. 9, 12); RQ4 chunk-size analysis (pp. 13-14)
notes: In-document task ranks chunks with a fixed cutoff (DCG@10) and counts a chunk relevant on any overlap with a gold paragraph, so larger chunks gain both coverage and relevance. In-corpus task is document ranking via MaxP (text amount not the retrieved unit). Explicitly treats chunk size as a possible confound (RQ4) via per-query correlations of chunk size with effectiveness (r up to 0.44 in-document), but does not equalise retrieved text. Paired t-tests vs best/worst.

headline_claim: "content-aware chunking significantly improves retrieval effectiveness over naive fixed-length splitting" (p. 1, Abstract)
evidence_location: Dense retrieval setup and relevance evaluation (p. 6); method table (p. 4); chunk length remark (p. 10); CI metrics in correlation analysis (p. 11)
notes: 36 strategies whose chunk sizes range from 50-token windows to paragraph groups, all compared at top-5. Each retrieved chunk is graded by an LLM judge for support of the reference answer, so longer chunks have more chances to be judged relevant. Notes that 'average chunk length alone is an incomplete predictor' (p. 10) but does not equalise or report retrieved text per strategy. nDCG CI bounds are computed (p. 11) but no pairwise tests are shown for the headline 'significantly' claim.

n_queries_per_dataset: not stated (documents per dataset in Table A.5)
headline_claim: "Methods with fewer but more coherent chunks (e.g., GraphSeg and Lumberchunker) achieve the strongest Recall@10 and Accuracy@5 ... chunk quality and structural coherence are more important than chunk quantity" (p. 7, Sec. 4)
evidence_location: Sec. 3 (p. 4: 'chunk sizes were not normalized across methods'); Sec. 3.1-3.2 (pp. 4-5); Sec. 4 (pp. 5-7); Table A.5 (p. 9)
notes: States explicitly that chunk sizes were not normalised across methods (p. 4). Relevance = chunk overlaps the answer span. The headline attributes the advantage of methods producing fewer (hence longer) chunks to 'coherence', while comparing at equal k: a direct instance of the uncontrolled text-amount confound. Generation context capped at 4,000 tokens. Failed configurations excluded (T/S markers).

All chunkers capped at 512 tokens; variable-length chunkers' mean lengths not reported (chunk counts are). SDs reported are spreads across chunkers, not uncertainty.

headline_claim: "Under the tested configuration, cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler strategies." (p. 1, Abstract)

notes: Retrieval depth (number of chunks) is not stated. Fixed and recursive chunkers target 150 words; cluster chunker targets 3 sentences x 1.2 slack, so lengths may differ but are not reported. Faithfulness failed in 44% of cases; results are medians/IQRs only.

headline_claim: "LumberChunker not only outperforms the most competitive baseline by 7.37% in retrieval performance (DCG@20) but also that, when integrated into a RAG pipeline, LumberChunker proves to be more effective than other chunking methods" (p. 1, Abstract)
evidence_location: Sec. 4 GutenQA and baselines (p. 3); Table 1 (p. 4); App. F Table 9 mean tokens per chunk (p. 12)
notes: Mean chunk lengths are reported (Table 9): LumberChunker 334 tokens vs Semantic 185, Paragraph 79, Proposition 12, Recursive 399, but all are compared at equal k, so e.g. at k=1 LumberChunker retrieves ~4x the text of paragraph chunks. Recursive chunks are longer than LumberChunker's and still score lower, so length does not explain every contrast. No uncertainty.
